angle: Style reference (fictional project): a CI cache shared across branches lets an untrusted pull request poison release builds.

threads.post:
A pull request from a fork could overwrite the build cache that release jobs restore.

example/forge keyed its CI cache on the lockfile hash only, not on the branch.
Same lockfile, same key: the fork's poisoned artifacts were restored into the tagged release.
The fix scopes cache keys to the ref and drops write access for fork workflows.
threads.reply:
The maintainers note the cache was never signed, so any job able to write a key could replace it. Cache restores are a trust boundary, not an optimisation.

Source: https://example.com/forge-postmortem

tiktok.title: How a shared CI cache leaked into a release build
tiktok.description: Fictional style reference. A fork's pull request wrote to a cache key that release jobs trusted. Scoping keys to the ref closes the hole. #cicd #supplychain

slides.heading: Your CI cache is part of your release
slides.body: A fork's pull request poisoned the artifacts of a tagged build.

slides.heading: How the poisoning worked
bullets: Cache key derived from the lockfile hash only
Fork workflow ran with write access to the cache
It saved modified build outputs under that key
The release job restored the same key and shipped them

slides.heading: What the postmortem gets right
bullets: Treats cache restore as untrusted input
Rebuilds release artifacts from a clean runner
Publishes the exact window of affected tags

slides.heading: Verdict
slides.body: Audit who can write each cache key your release jobs read. If the answer includes forks, the cache is an attack surface.
left: You cache build outputs in CI
